Family Health

Cleaner indoor air: ventilation, filters and masks for respiratory viruses

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Respiratory viruses, including the virus that causes COVID-19, can spread through particles people release while breathing, talking or coughing. Cleaner air reduces exposure, but a cool room, open window or air-cleaner label cannot prove that infection is impossible. Start with the room, its occupants and the equipment you can safely use.

Understand what cleaner air can do

Infectious particles can accumulate in shared indoor air, particularly in crowded or poorly ventilated spaces. Bringing in outdoor air dilutes them; filtration removes particles from air that passes through a filter. Neither measure instantly removes a fresh plume from someone nearby.

Laboratory or classroom simulations depend on their airflow, room layout and assumptions. A result from one model is not a universal percentage of viruses removed, and particle capture is not the same as a measured reduction in infections. Layer cleaner air with other appropriate precautions.

Bring in outdoor air when it is safe

Open windows or suitable doors to improve air exchange; openings on different sides can help. Even a partial opening may be useful. In uncomfortable weather, shorter openings may be more practical, but there is no single opening duration that makes every room safe.

Consider outdoor smoke or pollution, extreme temperatures, asthma triggers, security and falls before opening windows. Keep children away from unsafe openings. Do not prop open fire doors or interfere with building safety systems. When outdoor air is unsafe, prioritize suitable filtration and ask about safer ventilation options.

Direct airflow thoughtfully

A safely positioned fan at an open window can help move indoor air outside. Avoid directing a strong stream from one person toward another. Keep fans stable and protect children from blades, cords and accessible controls; follow the manufacturer's placement instructions.

Fans that only move the same indoor air do not supply outdoor air. Room mixing can help distribute cleaner air, but poorly arranged flows or barriers can leave stagnant areas. Ask building staff to assess outlets and layout rather than declaring every supply vent or doorway an infection hotspot.

Cooling is not necessarily ventilation

Many wall, window and split air conditioners mainly recirculate indoor air. Cooling or dehumidifying the room does not necessarily bring in fresh air. Other heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems combine outdoor air and recirculation: check what your actual system does.

Recirculated air can still be useful when it passes through effective, compatible filtration. Ask the building operator about outdoor-air supply, filter performance and operating hours. Do not modify dampers, ducts or controls yourself; extra outdoor air and longer operation affect energy use, humidity and comfort.

Upgrade central filters only if the system supports them

CDC recommends MERV 13 filtration, or the highest efficiency the system can accommodate without harming performance. MERV describes tested particle-capture efficiency; it is not a promise of protection for everyone in the room. Ask an HVAC professional about compatibility rather than choosing only the highest number.

A filter that is too restrictive can reduce airflow and strain operation. Correct dimensions, a good seal and timely replacement matter. Follow service instructions and keep air intakes and outlets clear. Most ordinary central systems cannot simply accept a HEPA filter as a direct replacement.

What HEPA means for small particles

HEPA filters capture particles; they are not simple sieves that let everything smaller than a stated size pass through. The often-quoted 0.3 micrometre figure describes a difficult test size, not the smallest particle captured. Smaller and larger particles can be collected efficiently too.

Viruses usually travel in respiratory particles rather than as isolated virus-sized objects. However, a filter's laboratory efficiency describes air passing through it, not every breath someone takes in a room. Airflow, leaks, placement and operating time still determine how much useful cleaning occurs.

Choose and position a portable cleaner

Look for a mechanical particle-filtering unit with a clean air delivery rate, or CADR, suitable for the room. Consider floor area, ceiling height and the speed you will actually tolerate. Smoke CADR is useful for fine-particle comparisons; a large advertised room area may assume conditions unlike yours.

Follow placement instructions, leave air inlets and outlets unobstructed and run the unit while the space is used. A suitable location near activity can help, but do not blow air from an ill person directly across others. One small unit will not necessarily clean several rooms or an entire open-plan building.

Work with building and budget limits

A windowless room is not automatically unventilated: it may receive outdoor air mechanically. Ask who maintains the system and whether it works for the current occupancy. If ventilation is inadequate, consider another space, fewer people, shorter visits or added suitable filtration while the problem is addressed.

Compare running costs, replacement filters, noise and maintenance as well as purchase price. Simple safe changes may help without replacing a whole system. Schools and workplaces need a responsible person, a service schedule and professional advice for equipment changes; published example prices are not local quotations.

Use air-change targets and monitors with care

CDC offers roughly five or more clean-air changes per hour, where possible, as a practical workplace guide. Outdoor ventilation and effective filtered-air delivery can contribute. It is not a universal household pass/fail threshold: room volume, occupancy, activity and vulnerability affect what is appropriate.

Carbon-dioxide readings can help investigate outdoor-air ventilation, but do not detect viruses or prove a room infection-free. Particle filters do not remove the carbon dioxide people exhale. A reassuring reading cannot replace assessment of crowding, close contact or whether the equipment is operating correctly.

Use fresh-air settings in vehicles

When sharing a car, open windows if conditions and road safety allow, and use the setting that draws in outdoor air rather than continuous recirculation. Check the vehicle manual or controls if the symbols are unclear. Protect children from unsafe window access.

Outdoor pollution, severe weather or other hazards can limit window opening; use a practical combination of ventilation and other precautions. Air conditioning alone does not establish that the cabin has good air exchange. Keep journeys and the number of occupants reasonable, especially when someone may be infectious.

Masks add protection that airflow cannot guarantee

A well-fitting mask can reduce particles released into the air and particles breathed in. Choose the most protective type you can comfortably wear correctly, covering nose and mouth. Well-fitting respirators such as N95 or KN95 generally provide better wearer protection than loose medical masks or cloth masks.

Fit and material both matter; softness or a tight weave alone does not establish a cloth mask's performance. Gaps allow leakage. A community fit check is not the same as occupational fit testing. A face shield alone does not replace a mask, even in a well-ventilated room.

Adapt the plan for children and household illness

Do not put a mask on a child under two. For older children, consider their ability to tolerate, put on and remove it safely, with appropriate supervision and local advice. Keep cleaner-air measures accessible for people who cannot safely use a mask rather than relying on masking alone.

If someone is unwell, avoid unnecessary close indoor contact and improve air in their room and shared areas when safe. Do not deliberately blow their room air into the rest of the home. Families with a pregnant person, young child or other vulnerable member may want extra layers and tailored clinical advice.

Treat ultraviolet and other devices cautiously

Professionally designed germicidal ultraviolet systems can supplement ventilation in some buildings. Design, installation and maintenance determine performance and safe exposure. This is a specialist building decision, not a recommendation to aim a household UV lamp at people or attempt a homemade air-disinfection system.

Avoid air cleaners that intentionally generate ozone. Be cautious with ionization or chemical air-treatment claims; ask for evidence of performance and safety in the actual setting. A device's registration or a dramatic laboratory claim does not establish that it safely prevents household infection.

Make a plan people can keep using

Identify the rooms used most, who may be at greater risk, how outdoor air enters and who checks filters or equipment. Choose changes that can run safely and consistently. Reassess when seasons, occupancy or room layout change rather than treating the initial purchase as the whole solution.

Cleaner air complements staying away from others when ill, appropriate vaccination and other current local prevention advice. It does not guarantee protection or replace care for someone who is sick. Ask a building professional about ventilation faults and a healthcare professional about individual illness or vulnerability.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask what outdoor air and filtration your actual room receives, who maintains it and whether changes are compatible.

Choose safe ventilation, correctly sized filtration and appropriate masks together, adjusting for children and vulnerable occupants.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps families turn indoor-air advice into questions for building staff and practical everyday choices. Personal medical advice and professional building assessment remain separate parts of that plan.

When to seek help

Keep windows, fans, cords and equipment safe around children. Do not modify building systems, expose people to household UV lamps or use ozone-generating cleaners. Cleaner air is prevention support, not treatment or proof that infection cannot occur.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Outdoor ventilation and particle filtration do different, complementary jobs.
  • Check the actual system; cool or recirculated air is not automatically fresh air.
  • Match filters and portable cleaners to equipment, room size and practical use.
  • Well-fitting masks add protection; face shields alone do not replace them.
  • Use safe, sustainable layers rather than a promise of zero infection risk.

Frequently asked questions

Does opening a window guarantee a safe room?

No. It can improve air exchange, but the effect depends on conditions, openings and occupants. Balance it with pollution, weather, security and child safety, and use other appropriate precautions.

Does air conditioning bring in fresh air?

Not always. Many wall or split units recirculate room air; some larger systems add outdoor air. Ask what your actual system provides and how it is maintained.

Are viruses too small for HEPA filters?

That is not a useful conclusion from virus size alone. HEPA captures very small particles, including respiratory particles carrying viruses. Its test efficiency is not a guarantee for every person in a room.

Can I put HEPA into any heating or cooling system?

No. Many central systems cannot handle its airflow resistance. Use the highest compatible filter advised for the system, or a suitably sized portable unit with its own fan.

Where should a portable cleaner go?

Follow its instructions, keep airflow unobstructed and choose a location serving the occupied area without blowing air directly from one person to another. Account for room size, ceiling height, noise and the speed you actually use.

How can I improve air in a shared car?

Use outdoor-air mode and open windows when safe. Do not assume cooling alone ventilates the cabin. Consider pollution, weather, passenger vulnerability and other protective measures.

Is a cloth mask or face shield enough?

Cloth masks generally offer less protection than well-fitting medical masks or respirators. Fit still matters with every type. A face shield alone is not a mask replacement, and children under two should not wear masks.

Do five air changes or a low CO2 reading prove there is no risk?

No. Air-change guidance is contextual, and CO2 is a ventilation clue rather than a virus detector. Neither proves that a room is infection-free or removes the need for other precautions.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
